paragraphs: A large rose tree stood near the entrance to the garden. The roses on it were white, but there were three gardeners busily painting them red. Alice thought this was very curious, and she went closer to watch. Just as she came up to them, she heard one of them say, “Watch out, Five! Don’t go splashing paint all over me like that!”
“I couldn’t help it,” said Five in a sulky tone. “Seven bumped my elbow.”
At which Seven looked up and said, “That’s right, Five! Always blame someone else!”
“You shouldn’t talk!” said Five. “I heard the Queen say just yesterday that you deserve to be beheaded!”
“What for?” said the one who had spoken first.
“That’s none of your business, Two!” said Seven.
“Yes, it is his business!” said Five. “And I’ll tell him. It was for bringing the cook tulip bulbs instead of onions.”

Seven flung down his brush and had just begun, “Well, of all the unfair things—” when his eye happened to fall on Alice, who was standing there watching them. He stopped himself suddenly. The others looked around too, and all of them bowed low.
“Could you tell me,” said Alice, a little timidly, “why you’re painting those roses?”

Five and Seven said nothing but looked at Two. Two began in a low voice, “Well, the thing is, Miss, this should have been a red rose tree, and we put a white one in by mistake. If the Queen found out, we’d all have our heads cut off, you see. So, Miss, we’re doing our best, before she comes, to—” At this moment Five, who had been looking anxiously across the garden, called out, “The Queen! The Queen!” and the three gardeners instantly threw themselves flat on their faces. There was a sound of many footsteps, and Alice looked around, eager to see the Queen.

First came ten soldiers carrying clubs. They were all shaped like the three gardeners: flat and rectangular, with their hands and feet at the corners. Next came the ten courtiers, decorated all over with diamonds, who walked two by two, like the soldiers. After these came the royal children, ten of them, and the little dears came skipping merrily along hand in hand, in pairs. They were all decorated with hearts. Next came the guests, mostly Kings and Queens, and among them Alice recognized the White Rabbit. He was talking in a nervous, hurried way, smiling at everything that was said, and went by without noticing her. Then came the Knave of Hearts, carrying the King’s crown on a crimson velvet cushion. And last of all in this grand procession came THE KING AND QUEEN OF HEARTS.

Alice wasn’t sure whether she should lie down on her face like the three gardeners, but she couldn’t remember ever hearing of such a rule at processions. “And besides,” she thought, “what would be the point of a procession if everyone had to lie on their faces so they couldn’t see it?” So she stood where she was and waited.
When the procession came level with Alice, they all stopped and looked at her, and the Queen said sternly, “Who is this?” She said it to the Knave of Hearts, who only bowed and smiled in reply.
“Idiot!” said the Queen, tossing her head impatiently. Turning to Alice, she went on, “What’s your name, child?”
“My name is Alice, if it please your Majesty,” said Alice very politely. But she added to herself, “Why, they’re only a pack of cards, after all. I don’t need to be afraid of them!”

“And who are these?” said the Queen, pointing to the three gardeners lying around the rose tree. You see, since they were lying on their faces, and the pattern on their backs was the same as the rest of the pack, she couldn’t tell whether they were gardeners, soldiers, courtiers, or three of her own children.
“How should I know?” said Alice, surprised at her own courage. “It’s none of my business.”
The Queen turned crimson with fury and, after glaring at her for a moment like a wild animal, screamed, “Off with her head! Off—”
“Nonsense!” said Alice, very loudly and firmly, and the Queen fell silent.
The King laid his hand on her arm and said timidly, “Consider, my dear: she is only a child!”
The Queen turned angrily away from him and said to the Knave, “Turn them over!”
The Knave did so, very carefully, with one foot.
“Get up!” said the Queen in a shrill, loud voice, and the three gardeners instantly jumped up and began bowing to the King, the Queen, the royal children, and everybody else.
“Stop that!” screamed the Queen. “You’re making me dizzy.” And then, turning to the rose tree, she went on, “What have you been doing here?”
“If it please your Majesty,” said Two, in a very humble tone, going down on one knee as he spoke, “we were trying—”

“I see!” said the Queen, who had meanwhile been examining the roses. “Off with their heads!” And the procession moved on, with three of the soldiers staying behind to execute the unfortunate gardeners, who ran to Alice for protection.

“You won’t be beheaded!” said Alice, and she put them into a large flowerpot that stood nearby. The three soldiers wandered around for a minute or two, looking for them, and then quietly marched off after the others.
“Are their heads off?” shouted the Queen.
“Their heads are gone, if it please your Majesty!” the soldiers shouted in reply.
“Good!” shouted the Queen. “Can you play croquet?”
The soldiers were silent and looked at Alice, because the question was obviously meant for her.
“Yes!” shouted Alice.
“Come on, then!” roared the Queen, and Alice joined the procession, wondering very much what would happen next.
“It’s—it’s a very fine day!” said a timid voice at her side. She was walking beside the White Rabbit, who was peeping anxiously into her face.
“Very,” said Alice. “Where’s the Duchess?”

“Hush! Hush!” said the Rabbit in a low, hurried tone. He looked anxiously over his shoulder as he spoke, then rose up on tiptoe, put his mouth close to her ear, and whispered, “She’s been sentenced to execution.”
“What for?” said Alice.
“Did you say ‘What a pity!’?” the Rabbit asked.
“No, I didn’t,” said Alice. “I don’t think it’s a pity at all. I said ‘What for?’”

“She boxed the Queen’s ears—” the Rabbit began. Alice let out a little scream of laughter. “Oh, hush!” the Rabbit whispered in a frightened tone. “The Queen will hear you! You see, she came rather late, and the Queen said—”

“Get to your places!” shouted the Queen in a voice of thunder, and people began running around in all directions, tumbling into each other. However, they got settled in a minute or two, and the game began. Alice thought she had never seen such a strange croquet ground in her life. It was all ridges and furrows. The balls were live hedgehogs, the mallets were live flamingos, and the soldiers had to bend over and stand on their hands and feet to make the arches.

The main difficulty Alice had at first was handling her flamingo. She managed to tuck its body comfortably enough under her arm, with its legs hanging down, but usually, just as she had gotten its neck nicely straightened out and was about to hit the hedgehog with its head, it would twist around and look up into her face with such a puzzled expression that she couldn’t help bursting out laughing. And when she had gotten its head down and was about to start again, it was very annoying to find that the hedgehog had unrolled itself and was crawling away. On top of all this, there was usually a ridge or furrow in the way wherever she wanted to send the hedgehog, and since the bent-over soldiers were always getting up and walking off to other parts of the ground, Alice soon concluded that it was a very difficult game indeed.

The players all played at once without waiting for turns, quarreling all the while and fighting over the hedgehogs. Very soon the Queen was in a furious rage and went stamping about, shouting, “Off with his head!” or “Off with her head!” about once a minute.

Alice began to feel very uneasy. To be sure, she hadn’t had any argument with the Queen yet, but she knew it could happen any minute. “And then,” she thought, “what would become of me? They’re dreadfully fond of beheading people here. The great wonder is that anyone is left alive!”

She was looking around for some way to escape, and wondering if she could get away without being seen, when she noticed a curious shape in the air. It puzzled her very much at first, but after watching it for a minute or two, she made it out to be a grin, and she said to herself, “It’s the Cheshire Cat. Now I’ll have somebody to talk to.”
“How are you getting on?” said the Cat, as soon as there was enough mouth to speak with.

Alice waited until the eyes appeared and then nodded. “There’s no use speaking to it,” she thought, “until its ears have come, or at least one of them.” A minute later the whole head appeared, and then Alice put down her flamingo and began telling it about the game, feeling very glad she had someone to listen to her. The Cat seemed to think there was enough of it in sight now, and no more of it appeared.

“I don’t think they play fair at all,” Alice began, in rather a complaining tone, “and they all quarrel so dreadfully you can’t hear yourself speak. And they don’t seem to have any particular rules. At least, if there are any, nobody pays attention to them. And you can’t imagine how confusing it is with everything being alive. For instance, the arch I’m supposed to go through next is walking around at the other end of the ground. And I would have croqueted the Queen’s hedgehog just now, only it ran away when it saw mine coming!”
“How do you like the Queen?” said the Cat in a low voice.
“Not at all,” said Alice. “She’s so extremely—” Just then she noticed that the Queen was right behind her, listening, so she went on, “—likely to win that it’s hardly worth finishing the game.”
The Queen smiled and moved on.
“Who are you talking to?” said the King, coming up to Alice and looking at the Cat’s head with great curiosity.
“It’s a friend of mine, a Cheshire Cat,” said Alice. “Allow me to introduce it.”
“I don’t like the look of it at all,” said the King. “However, it may kiss my hand if it likes.”
“I’d rather not,” the Cat remarked.
“Don’t be impertinent,” said the King, “and don’t look at me like that!” He got behind Alice as he spoke.
“A cat may look at a king,” said Alice. “I read that in some book, but I don’t remember which.”
“Well, it has to be removed,” said the King very firmly, and he called to the Queen, who was passing at that moment, “My dear! I wish you would have this cat removed!”
The Queen had only one way of settling all difficulties, great or small. “Off with his head!” she said, without even looking around.
“I’ll fetch the executioner myself,” said the King eagerly, and he hurried off.

Alice thought she might as well go back and see how the game was going, since she could hear the Queen’s voice in the distance, screaming with rage. She had already heard her sentence three of the players to be executed for missing their turns, and she didn’t like the look of things at all, because the game was in such confusion that she never knew whether it was her turn or not. So she went to look for her hedgehog.

The hedgehog was fighting with another hedgehog, which seemed to Alice an excellent chance to croquet one of them with the other. The only problem was that her flamingo had gone over to the other side of the garden, where Alice could see it trying in a helpless way to fly up into a tree.

By the time she had caught the flamingo and brought it back, the fight was over and both hedgehogs were out of sight. “But it doesn’t matter much,” thought Alice, “since all the arches are gone from this side of the ground.” So she tucked it under her arm so it couldn’t escape again and went back for a little more conversation with her friend.

When she got back to the Cheshire Cat, she was surprised to find quite a large crowd gathered around it. An argument was going on between the executioner, the King, and the Queen, who were all talking at once, while everyone else was silent and looked very uncomfortable.

The moment Alice appeared, all three appealed to her to settle the question, and they repeated their arguments to her. Since they all spoke at once, though, she found it very hard to make out exactly what they were saying.

The executioner’s argument was that you couldn’t cut off a head unless there was a body to cut it off from, that he had never had to do such a thing before, and that he wasn’t going to start at his age.
The King’s argument was that anything with a head could be beheaded, and that you shouldn’t talk nonsense.

The Queen’s argument was that if something wasn’t done about it in no time, she would have everyone executed, all around. (It was this last remark that had made the whole party look so grave and anxious.)
Alice could think of nothing else to say but, “It belongs to the Duchess. You’d better ask her about it.”
“She’s in prison,” the Queen said to the executioner. “Fetch her here.” And the executioner went off like an arrow.

The Cat’s head began fading away the moment he was gone, and by the time he came back with the Duchess, it had disappeared entirely. So the King and the executioner ran wildly up and down looking for it, while the rest of the party went back to the game.
